newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia vote may be delayed by up to a month.
newsitem.headline: Liberia vote may be delayed by up to a month.

text.p: Elections in Liberia, tentatively scheduled for May 30, may be postponed by up to a month to give more time for preparations, the independent electoral commission said on Saturday.
Nine parties have registered for the vote, part of a peace plan which ended a civil war that killed more than 150,000 people.
The postponement has been agreed by ministers of neighbouring countries which brokered the peace, by the electoral commission and by the political parties.
"We will not hold elections when it is impossible to do so," Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi said.
The electoral commission, preparing for both legislative and presidential elections, needs to recruit thousands of registrars.

"Prospects for holding elections as scheduled are very good...A change of date must be very slight. We are not trying to create new elections here," Ghana's deputy foreign minister Victor Gbeho told reporters.
Election commission chairman Henry Andrews said the vote would cost $12 million, of which 80 percent would come from international donors and the rest from the interim government.
Presidential candidates include Charles Taylor, the man who launched the seven-year war in December 1989, and his sometimes foe Alhaji Kromahand Kromah.
Taylor, who repeatedly tried and failed to take the capital by force, will run under the banner of his National Patriotic Party.
Kromah, a Mandingo whose stronghold is in the west, will represent his All Liberia Coalition Party.

The other main warlords, Roosevelt Johnson and George Boley, will not be running. Both come from the Krahn ethnic group which seized power in 1980, breaking the stranglehold of descendants of freed American slaves who founded the nation in 1847.
As many as half of Liberia's pre-war population of 2.5 million people are displaced or have fled abroad.
